headline: OKC looks like red dirt, Route 66 neon and Plains Deco, under the Thunder's sunset
summary: Oklahoma City's art lives in small, fiercely local districts, not on one famous mural wall. The street look is mid-century roadside: Route 66 neon, hand-painted brick signs, Art Deco. The Thunder's blue, sunset orange and yellow already work as the civic palette. Lead with local makers and with Native and Black Oklahoma artists, and skip the Land Run and Western cliches.

insights.title: The districts are the scene
insights.detail: The Plaza District is on NW 16th, anchored by the Plaza District Association and its mural program and festivals. The Paseo Arts District has Spanish Pueblo Revival bungalows and working studios. Automobile Alley has its own look too. Locals identify with a district more than with a citywide art brand.
insights.implication: Brief a district-by-district capsule or collab series (Plaza, Paseo, Deep Deuce) instead of one generic OKC graphic. District names work as small-run graphic titles.

insights.title: Red clay below, flag blue above
insights.detail: Oklahoma clay reads as a deep oxide red, and the state flag's field is a flat sky blue. With the Thunder's blue and sunset orange, they sit very close to the team's own palette. Red dirt also names a whole local music and apparel idiom.
insights.implication: A red-clay colorway (washed, garment-dyed look) next to Thunder blue is a premium alternative to the default blue and orange, and it stays true to the place.

insights.title: Route 66 neon and Deco set the type
insights.detail: The city remembers its signs. Neon runs down Route 66 (Pops on the Arcadia stretch, with its giant soda-bottle sign, plus motel and diner script). Automobile Alley has showroom lettering. Art Deco and Streamline Moderne buildings mark downtown and Tulsa (Boston Avenue Methodist Church, Philtower). Hand-painted ghost signs and brick wall lettering are common in Bricktown and the Plaza.
insights.implication: Use script-and-block neon lettering, outlined slab type and stepped Deco geometry for graphics and jersey numbers. Tie it to the Route 66 centennial (2026) only after licensing is checked.

insights.title: Native design: the strongest source, the highest risk
insights.detail: Oklahoma's 39 tribal nations are the state's deepest design heritage: Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee, Osage, Kiowa, Comanche and many more. Living artists include Yatika Starr Fields (Cherokee/Osage/Muscogee, a muralist and painter based in Tulsa). The Red Earth Festival in Oklahoma City is a long-standing venue for Native artists, and the state flag is built on an Osage battle shield.
insights.implication: Pay and credit a Native artist or nation-approved partner for a real collaboration. Don't lift regalia, ceremonial patterns or tribal symbols as decoration, and keep Native work out of team-branded graphics without that partnership.

insights.title: Black Oklahoma artists own the Deep Deuce story
insights.detail: Deep Deuce (Deep Second) was the Black jazz and business district that shaped Charlie Christian and Ralph Ellison. Northeast OKC and Tulsa's Greenwood district carry mural and memorial work around Black Wall Street. These stories are tied to real loss and recovery, and local Black artists, not outside brands, own the narrative.
insights.implication: If you use it, start with community partners and make Black Oklahoma artists the lead creators, with revenue share. Greenwood and the 1921 massacre are not a decorative theme.

insights.title: Thunder iconography is already the shared civic art
insights.detail: Thunder blue, sunset orange and yellow, the thunderbolt-and-basketball marks and the Loud City crowd culture are painted on walls, murals and shop fronts across the metro. Thunder fan art sells heavily through local print makers, gig posters, Plaza shops and fan markets.
insights.implication: Frame local artist collabs on official product as a flip on Thunder colors, not a competing identity. Let artists reinterpret the team's sunset and storm sky.

places.name: Plaza District
places.why: The city's densest cluster of murals, indie shops, studios and gig-poster culture, with a long-running mural and festival program.

places.name: Paseo Arts District
places.why: Spanish Pueblo Revival studios and galleries with working artists. Home of the Paseo Arts Festival.

places.name: Oklahoma Contemporary Arts Center
places.why: The state's leading contemporary art venue, with studios, exhibitions and a purpose-built campus that anchors Midtown design culture.

places.name: Oklahoma City Museum of Art
places.why: Houses a major Chihuly glass collection, including the 50-plus-foot Chihuly tower that is a recognizable city image.

places.name: Factory Obscura
places.why: A locally founded immersive and interactive art collective whose work has toured nationally. A credible collaborator for experiential launches.

places.name: Automobile Alley
places.why: Former auto showrooms with period lettering and murals, now a design and retail corridor.

places.name: Deep Deuce
places.why: Historic Black jazz district with markers and murals recalling Charlie Christian and Ralph Ellison.

places.name: Pops 66
places.why: A huge neon soda-bottle sign and glass-bottle wall make it the most photographed piece of Oklahoma roadside graphic design.

places.name: Tulsa Art Deco district and Philbrook Museum
places.why: Tulsa has the state's richest Art Deco stock and a deep arts bench, including the Tulsa Artist Fellowship.

places.name: Red Earth Festival
places.why: Annual juried showcase for Native American artists and dancers, and a respected way into Native art networks.

people.name: Yatika Starr Fields
people.why: Internationally exhibited Oklahoma muralist whose bold, color-saturated large walls make him a credible Native collaborator, if engaged on his terms.

people.name: Factory Obscura
people.why: Homegrown OKC team behind interactive installations. A fit for experiential or store-environment work.

people.name: Oklahoma Contemporary Arts Center
people.why: A natural partner for artist-in-residence or studio collaboration programs with local makers.

people.name: Plaza District Association
people.why: Organizes mural commissions and festivals. Call first for walls and pop-ups in the Plaza.

people.name: Paseo Arts Association
people.why: Runs the Paseo Arts Festival and represents resident studio artists.

people.name: Tulsa Artist Fellowship
people.why: Brings working artists to Tulsa and keeps them there. A pipeline for credible state-level collaborators.

people.name: Charlie Christian and Ralph Ellison (honored legacies)
people.why: Their legacy is a reference for district stories. Any use needs an estate and community conversation, not a graphic lift.

moments.name: Festival of the Arts
moments.why: Long-running downtown outdoor art festival with the broadest local audience. It overlaps the NBA playoffs.

moments.name: Paseo Arts Festival
moments.why: Neighborhood-scale juried art fair in the Paseo. The Thunder playoff run often overlaps.

moments.name: Red Earth Festival
moments.why: Major Native arts and dance gathering in Oklahoma City.

moments.name: Oklahoma State Fair
moments.why: Peak display of Oklahoma vernacular graphics: midway lettering, livestock and craft ribbons.

moments.name: Plaza District Festival and mural events
moments.why: Neighborhood block party with live painting and local makers, close to preseason.

moments.name: Opening night and NBA Cup nights
moments.timing: Oct 20 start, Cup group play Fridays from Oct 30
moments.why: The Thunder open at San Antonio, and home Cup Fridays give early windows for district pop-ups and mural reveals.

moments.name: Juneteenth in Northeast OKC and Greenwood (Tulsa)
moments.why: The most important annual moment for Black Oklahoma art and memory, led by local organizations.

vocabulary.meaning: The Thunder fan identity at Paycom Center, named for the crowd's volume.
The team's rallying call and fan phrase.
Oklahoma's clay soil, and shorthand for a local music and lifestyle idiom.
How locals refer to the two arts districts, without the word "district".
Local name for the historic Black district along Second Street east of downtown.
The canal-side entertainment district of converted brick warehouses. Locals rarely call it art.
A self-applied identity locals wear with pride. Its Dust Bowl history is not a joke for outsiders.
The Thunder's bison mascot, a local favorite for kids and fan art.

designCues.cue: Thunder sunset orange against prairie sky blue
designCues.source: Thunder sunset orange, which also echoes Oklahoma sunsets and Route 66 neon
designCues.use: Make it the lead accent on a City Edition or lifestyle capsule, paired with Thunder blue for a coherent local palette.

designCues.cue: Thunder blue as the sky field
designCues.source: Thunder primary color and the sky-blue state flag field
designCues.use: Base color for tees, warm-ups and shorts.
Garment-dyed or washed fleece and tees with an earthy finish, plus a tone-on-tone dirt-splatter print.

designCues.cue: Neon script and outlined slab lettering
designCues.source: Route 66 motel, diner and soda signs; Automobile Alley showroom lettering
designCues.use: Wordmark lockups and number treatments with a glow outline, in reflective or glow-in-the-dark ink.

designCues.source: Downtown OKC and Tulsa Deco architecture
designCues.use: Tonal jacquard or embossed trim on jackets and jersey side panels.

designCues.source: Storm-front skies, tornado-season horizons and the Thunder name
designCues.use: Gradient fades on shorts and hoodies. Avoid literal tornado or disaster imagery.

designCues.source: Ghost signs on Bricktown, Plaza and Automobile Alley walls
designCues.use: Distressed print finish on retro graphic tees. Keep it legible.

productHooks: District capsule series (Plaza, Paseo, Deep Deuce), one local artist per release, credited on the hangtag and paid royalties.
Route 66 neon-script warm-up or fleece in Thunder sunset orange and dark navy, timed to the Route 66 centennial year.
Red-clay garment-dyed hoodie and tee set with a restrained Thunder-blue mark, for fan and lifestyle retail.
Native artist co-created collection, led by a Native designer with full credit and payment, and released with a community event rather than a drop alone.
Court-side or store-environment art installations for launch events, commissioned from Factory Obscura or Plaza District artists.
watchouts: Tribal symbols, regalia, war bonnets and the Osage shield are not decoration. Engage Native artists directly and pay them.
Land Run, Dust Bowl and cowboy imagery reads as cliche, and the Land Run reads as dispossession. Avoid it, or get Native input.
The Oklahoma City National Memorial and Tulsa's 1921 massacre are memorials, not graphic themes.
Route 66 signage, Pops and similar landmarks may carry trademark or sign-owner rights. License before reproducing.
The Plaza and Paseo associations and individual muralists own their murals. Photos of walls on product need artist permission.
